articles.title: Are we getting smarter with AI, or simply thinking less?
articles.excerpt: What the research says about AI, productivity and learning, and how to use AI in a way that keeps your own thinking sharp.
articles.content:
Imagine a young professional who uses ChatGPT to write emails, summarise reports, develop presentations, analyse business problems, and prepare for meetings. In one working day, he accomplishes what might previously have taken him three. His employer is pleased. His productivity has improved, and he has more time to attend to other responsibilities.

Six months later, he is asked to prepare a strategic recommendation without AI. He struggles to organise his thoughts, develop an argument, and arrive at a defensible conclusion.

Has he become more intelligent because he can accomplish more, or has he become more dependent on a system that does much of his thinking for him?

This is one of the most important questions emerging from the artificial intelligence revolution, and I suspect we are paying far less attention to it than we should.

For years, the conversation around AI has revolved around productivity. How much faster can we work? How many tasks can we automate? How much money can businesses save? These are legitimate questions, particularly for organisations under pressure to improve performance.

But there is another question worth investigating: what happens to human intelligence when the effort required to think becomes increasingly optional?

In 2025, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University surveyed 319 knowledge workers about their use of generative AI. They collected 936 examples of AI-assisted tasks and found that greater confidence in AI was associated with less reported critical thinking. Interestingly, workers who had greater confidence in their own abilities reported more critical thinking.

The study did not establish that AI was making people less intelligent. It revealed something worth examining: the relationship between our confidence in technology and the effort we invest in our own thinking.

To understand why this matters, we need to look at how human intelligence develops, what AI is doing to the process, and what we might be sacrificing in our pursuit of efficiency.

The difference between getting answers and developing intelligence

Think about the last time you struggled to understand a difficult concept.

Perhaps it was a mathematical problem, a philosophical argument, or a complicated business decision. You read through the material, tried different approaches, made mistakes, and eventually arrived at an understanding.

Something happened during that process beyond finding the correct answer.

You developed your capacity to reason through similar problems.

Psychologists have studied this phenomenon for decades. One relevant concept is desirable difficulties, associated with the work of cognitive psychologist Robert Bjork. The idea is that certain difficulties during learning can improve long-term retention and transfer, even when they make the immediate learning experience feel slower.

This explains why attempting to recall something from memory can be more beneficial than repeatedly reading the answer. It also helps explain why working through a problem may produce more durable learning than watching someone else solve it.

Now introduce AI into the picture.

A student who previously spent forty minutes working through a difficult problem can receive a complete explanation in seconds. A marketer struggling to develop a campaign strategy can generate ten possible directions with a single prompt. A manager can ask AI to analyse a business problem and recommend a course of action.

The immediate result may be impressive. The user gets something useful, often much faster.

But the intellectual benefit depends on what happens next.

Does the student examine the explanation and attempt the problem independently? Does the marketer evaluate the assumptions behind the suggested strategies? Does the manager understand why one recommendation is better than another?

There is a meaningful difference between possessing an answer and developing the capacity to produce or evaluate one.

And that distinction becomes increasingly important when answers are cheap.

The productivity numbers are impressive. The learning numbers are more complicated.

We have good reasons to be excited about AI's economic potential.

In a study published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2025, researchers Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond examined the introduction of a generative AI assistant among 5,172 customer-support agents.

Access to AI increased productivity, measured by issues resolved per hour, by an average of 15%. The benefits varied considerably between workers, with less experienced employees generally gaining more. The researchers also found suggestive evidence that AI helped newer workers learn effective practices from more experienced colleagues.

This is important because it challenges the assumption that AI assistance necessarily weakens human competence. In some environments, AI may help people acquire knowledge and perform at levels that previously required years of experience.

Now consider a different study.

In 2025, researcher André Barcaui conducted a randomised controlled trial involving 120 undergraduate students learning about artificial intelligence. One group used ChatGPT as a study aid, while another used traditional study methods.

Forty-five days later, the students took an unexpected knowledge-retention test.

The traditional study group scored 68.5%, compared with 57.5% for the ChatGPT-assisted group, a difference of 11 percentage points.

The researchers concluded that unrestricted ChatGPT use may undermine long-term retention by reducing the mental effort involved in learning. This was one study with a particular group of students, so we should be careful about generalising its findings to every learning environment.

Still, the two studies raise an interesting possibility.

AI can improve immediate performance while producing different effects on the knowledge people develop along the way.

We should therefore be asking two questions whenever we introduce AI into a learning or working environment.

How much better does it help people perform today? And what capabilities are they developing that will remain useful tomorrow?

The hidden cost of cognitive offloading

Human beings have always found ways to reduce the mental effort required to accomplish tasks.

We use calculators for arithmetic, calendars to remember appointments, maps to navigate unfamiliar places, and search engines to retrieve information.

Psychologists call this cognitive offloading: using external tools or processes to reduce the demands placed on our internal cognitive resources.

It is one reason we can accomplish complex tasks without keeping every piece of information in our heads.

Consider a pilot using instruments to navigate an aircraft. The instruments provide information that would be difficult or impossible to obtain through human perception alone. Their usefulness depends partly on the pilot's ability to interpret them and respond appropriately.

AI introduces a more complicated form of offloading because it can participate in activities we traditionally associate with thinking itself.

It can construct arguments, generate hypotheses, interpret evidence, write explanations, and recommend decisions.

Suppose you are preparing a marketing strategy for a new business.

You could spend several hours researching customers, identifying competitors, examining buying behaviour, and developing possible positioning strategies.

Or you could describe the business to ChatGPT and ask it to produce a complete marketing strategy.

The second approach may save time. It might even produce a better initial document.

But imagine that the strategy fails after implementation.

Would you understand the assumptions that led to the recommendations? Could you identify where the analysis went wrong? Would you know which conclusions to revisit?

This is where the danger of excessive cognitive offloading becomes apparent.

When we outsource the intellectual process without understanding it, we may lose the ability to interrogate the result.

And in business, the cost of a poorly understood recommendation can be substantial.

When confidence in AI replaces confidence in judgment

Let's return to the Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study.

The researchers found that workers who trusted AI more tended to report less critical-thinking effort during AI-assisted tasks. They also observed that AI changed the nature of the thinking workers performed.

Instead of spending as much effort producing information themselves, workers increasingly focused on verifying, integrating, and supervising AI-generated material.

This shift deserves attention.

Imagine a financial analyst preparing an investment recommendation. Previously, she might have gathered information, constructed a model, evaluated competing assumptions, and developed her conclusion.

With AI, parts of that process can happen almost immediately.

Her responsibility then moves toward evaluating the model's output, checking assumptions, and determining whether the recommendation makes sense.

That can be a sophisticated form of work. In fact, it may require more judgment than producing the original calculations.

The problem emerges when the analyst lacks the expertise necessary to evaluate what the system produces.

A convincing explanation can create an illusion of understanding. A well-structured report can make weak reasoning appear credible. An authoritative tone can encourage us to accept conclusions we have barely examined.

I find this particularly interesting because it exposes a weakness in how we often measure intelligence at work.

We celebrate the person who produces the report fastest, generates the most ideas, or completes the greatest number of tasks.

Yet the person who can explain why a recommendation is wrong may be considerably more valuable than the person who generated it in thirty seconds.

The ability to recognise a bad answer becomes more important as the cost of producing plausible answers approaches zero.

Even productivity can be an illusion

There is another complication in the assumption that AI always makes us more productive.

In July 2025, the research organisation METR published a randomised study examining how experienced open-source software developers performed when using AI tools.

The researchers studied 16 developers completing 246 tasks in software repositories they knew well.

Before beginning, the developers predicted that AI would reduce their task completion time by approximately 24%.

The actual result was surprising.

The developers completed their tasks 19% more slowly when allowed to use AI.

Even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them faster.

There are limitations to this finding. The study involved a small number of experienced developers, specific software projects, and AI tools available in early 2025. It would be unreasonable to conclude that AI slows down software development generally.

What interests me is the gap between perceived productivity and measured productivity.

We may feel productive because AI makes certain activities easier. We generate more material, receive faster responses, and experience less friction.

But producing more material is only one part of accomplishing valuable work.

A business can generate twenty marketing campaigns in an afternoon and still fail to understand its customers. A manager can produce detailed strategic documents without resolving the organisation's underlying problems. A student can complete assignments efficiently while retaining very little of what was studied.

The ease of producing something can distort our perception of how much we have accomplished.

And when that happens, productivity becomes difficult to distinguish from activity.

What happens when the next generation learns to think with AI?

This is where the conversation becomes particularly important for education and the future of work.

Think about how people traditionally develop professional expertise.

A junior lawyer spends years researching cases, examining arguments, and drafting documents. A young designer learns by creating imperfect designs, receiving feedback, and improving them. A marketing associate develops judgment by studying customers, making recommendations, and observing what happens when those recommendations meet reality.

These activities involve mistakes, repetition, and the gradual accumulation of experience.

Now imagine that AI performs much of the preliminary work.

The lawyer receives a draft argument. The designer gets twenty design concepts. The marketer obtains a complete campaign proposal.

Their work may become more efficient, and the quality of their immediate output may improve.

But how will they develop the judgment required to supervise increasingly sophisticated AI systems?

An experienced professional can often recognise a poor recommendation because years of practice have developed their intuition. A beginner may accept the same recommendation because it sounds convincing.

This creates a possible problem for organisations.

If we automate too many of the activities through which beginners become experts, we may eventually struggle to produce the experts required to supervise the automation.

There is no reason to assume this outcome is inevitable. The customer-support study discussed earlier suggests AI can accelerate learning by making effective practices more accessible.

The important question is how we design the learning experience.

An AI assistant that explains its reasoning, challenges assumptions, and helps a junior employee work through a problem may contribute to professional development. A system that simply completes every task may produce a different outcome.

Organisations should therefore evaluate AI adoption partly by its effects on employee development.

A business that saves twenty hours of work this month but gradually weakens its employees' ability to solve unfamiliar problems may be creating a cost that will only become visible years later.

Learning to think with machines

I believe the most useful response to these concerns is to become more deliberate about how we use AI.

For individuals, this begins with understanding the difference between using AI to complete a task and using AI to improve our ability to complete that task.

If you are learning a new concept, try explaining it yourself before asking AI to evaluate your understanding. Ask the system to identify weaknesses in your explanation and challenge you with questions.

If you are developing a business strategy, begin by articulating your own assumptions. Use AI to examine competing possibilities, introduce relevant evidence, and identify considerations you may have overlooked.

If you are writing an article, develop your central argument before using AI to test its logic, research its claims, or explore alternative interpretations.

And when AI produces something important, ask yourself whether you understand it well enough to defend it.

For organisations, the challenge extends beyond individual habits.

Managers need to think carefully about which tasks employees should continue performing independently, especially during the early stages of professional development.

AI literacy training should include evaluating evidence, recognising limitations, and understanding the consequences of decisions. Teams also need meaningful ways to measure whether AI improves the quality of their work, alongside any gains in speed.

One practical exercise I would recommend is occasionally asking employees to explain an AI-assisted recommendation without referring to the original output.

What assumptions informed the recommendation? What evidence supports it? Under what circumstances might it fail?

Their answers can reveal how deeply they understand the work they are presenting.

These practices require judgment about the task. There is little educational value in manually repeating routine activities that contribute nothing to learning. But there is considerable value in retaining the intellectual effort through which competence develops.

The future belongs to people who can think about thinking

I have been thinking about what it will mean to be intelligent in a world where increasingly capable machines can perform activities once considered evidence of intelligence.

For a long time, access to information conferred an advantage. People who knew more could often do more.

The internet changed that relationship by making enormous amounts of information accessible to almost anyone with a connection.

Artificial intelligence is changing it again.

We can now interact with systems that organise information, generate explanations, analyse problems, and produce sophisticated intellectual work.

This makes certain capabilities more accessible. It also raises the value of understanding which problems deserve attention, what evidence should be trusted, and how competing considerations should inform a decision.

I suspect the future of human intelligence will depend increasingly on these abilities.

There is something ironic about building machines that can perform more cognitive work while paying insufficient attention to how human beings develop the capacity to think.

Perhaps the greatest danger is becoming so accustomed to receiving answers that we gradually lose our curiosity about how those answers were produced.

The evidence is still developing, and the long-term effects of generative AI on human cognition remain uncertain. We have studies showing productivity gains, evidence of learning benefits in some settings, and findings that raise concerns about retention, dependence, and critical thinking.

Together, they suggest that the consequences of AI depend considerably on how we use it.

As we continue integrating artificial intelligence into our lives, schools, and organisations, I think we should pay as much attention to the development of human intelligence as we do to the capabilities of our machines.

The next time you ask AI to think through a problem for you, consider whether the process could also help you become better at thinking through similar problems yourself.

That may be one of the most valuable questions we can ask in the age of artificial intelligence.

Authentic Intelligence The Art of Thinking Clearly

References and further reading

  1. Lee, H.-P., et al. (2025). The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking. CHI 2025. https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778
  2. Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D., & Raymond, L. R. (2025). Generative AI at Work. The Quarterly Journal of Economics. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044
  3. Barcaui, A. (2025). ChatGPT as a Cognitive Crutch: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial on Knowledge Retention. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590291125010186
  4. Becker, J., et al. (2025). Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity. METR. https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/

articles.title: Why Good Products Fail: The Psychology of What People Choose to Buy
articles.excerpt: Why customers choose what feels safe, familiar and easy to buy, and what a business should study before it spends on another campaign.
articles.content:
Imagine spending two years developing a product. You have studied the market, invested your savings, hired competent people, and built something that works remarkably well. The product is affordable, the design is impressive, and early users have given positive feedback.

You launch it with considerable excitement, expecting customers to recognise its value.

Six months later, sales are disappointing.

Meanwhile, a competitor with what you consider an inferior product is selling thousands of units. Their customers seem satisfied, their business is growing, and you cannot understand why people keep choosing them.

It is tempting to conclude that customers don't know what is good for them.

But perhaps the more interesting question is whether you understand what customers are buying in the first place.

In 2005, Clayton Christensen, Scott Cook, and Taddy Hall published an article in Harvard Business Review examining why so many new products failed despite extensive market research and substantial marketing investments. They cited estimates that more than 90% of new consumer products failed, although such figures depend heavily on how failure is defined and measured.

Their central argument was that businesses frequently misunderstand the circumstances that cause people to purchase products.

Two decades later, the problem remains relevant.

Companies have access to sophisticated customer analytics, artificial intelligence, behavioural data, and increasingly precise advertising tools. Yet developing a commercially successful product remains difficult.

I think part of the explanation lies in how we understand consumer behaviour.

Businesses often evaluate their products through the qualities they have built into them. Customers evaluate those products through the circumstances of their own lives, the alternatives available to them, and the consequences they expect from choosing one option over another.

The value a business creates and the value a customer perceives are related, but they are not necessarily the same thing.

Understanding that difference may be one of the most important lessons in marketing.

People buy progress, even when they are buying milkshakes

One of my favourite illustrations of consumer behaviour comes from Clayton Christensen's research into what became known as the Jobs to Be Done theory.

Christensen described a fast-food company trying to increase milkshake sales. Its marketing team had gathered customer information, developed demographic profiles, and asked consumers how the milkshakes could be improved.

The company made changes based on the feedback, but sales barely improved.

Researchers subsequently approached the problem differently. They observed when customers purchased milkshakes, what they were doing, and the circumstances surrounding those purchases.

They discovered something interesting.

A substantial proportion of milkshakes were purchased early in the morning by people travelling to work.

These customers wanted something that would keep them occupied during a long commute, satisfy their hunger, and be convenient to consume while driving.

The milkshake was competing with bananas, bagels, doughnuts, and other possible breakfast options.

Suddenly, the problem looked different.

The business had been thinking about how to make a better milkshake. Its customers were trying to make a boring morning commute more pleasant while managing their hunger.

Christensen described this through the idea that customers hire products to accomplish particular jobs.

The milkshake story is an illustrative business case rather than a controlled experiment, but its underlying insight is useful.

Consider someone buying a laptop.

The manufacturer may emphasise processor speed, storage capacity, screen resolution, and battery performance.

But a university student may be looking for a reliable device that can survive four years of school. A designer may prioritise software compatibility. A consultant may want something lightweight that looks professional during client meetings.

They are buying the same category of product for different reasons.

This is why a business can build something technically impressive and still struggle to attract customers.

It may have improved the product without adequately understanding the problem people wanted solved.

The best product doesn't always feel like the safest choice

Imagine you need to purchase a new smartphone.

You have two options.

The first comes from a familiar brand. You have used its products before, know people who own them, and can easily find repair centres and accessories.

The second comes from a relatively unknown manufacturer. Its specifications are better, its price is lower, and its design is attractive.

Which would you choose?

Your decision may depend on how much you know about the second manufacturer, how important reliability is to you, and what might happen if the phone develops a fault.

This introduces a concept that has been studied in consumer research for decades: perceived risk.

Consumers make decisions under uncertainty. Before buying a product, they cannot always know whether it will perform as promised, how long it will last, or whether the seller will honour its commitments.

They therefore rely on signals that help them estimate the likelihood of a satisfactory outcome.

A familiar brand, a trusted recommendation, a credible warranty, and a history of reliable service can all influence that assessment.

This helps explain why consumers sometimes pay more for products that appear technically similar to cheaper alternatives.

The additional money may purchase something beyond the product's immediate functional features. It may reduce the uncertainty surrounding the purchase.

Think about choosing a hospital, hiring a consultant, or selecting a contractor to build your house.

In each case, the consequences of making a poor decision can be significant.

You may be willing to pay a premium for a provider with a strong reputation, credible evidence of competence, and a history of delivering satisfactory results.

For businesses, this has an important implication.

Improving the product is valuable. But customers must also have sufficient reason to believe that the product will deliver what it promises.

A technically superior offering with weak credibility may struggle against an established alternative that feels safer.

Why familiarity has economic value

There is a psychological reason familiar brands often enjoy an advantage.

Human beings cannot carefully evaluate every available option whenever they need to make a purchase.

Imagine walking into a supermarket to buy toothpaste.

You could examine every brand, compare ingredients, read customer reviews, investigate manufacturing standards, and calculate the relative value of each product.

But you probably won't.

You may simply pick a brand you recognise, particularly if it has served you well before.

Psychologists refer to one relevant phenomenon as the mere-exposure effect. In a 1968 paper, Robert Zajonc demonstrated that repeated exposure to stimuli could increase people's positive evaluations of them under certain conditions.

The finding has since influenced how researchers understand familiarity, preference, and advertising.

Repeated exposure does not guarantee that someone will like or purchase a product. Negative experiences, poor quality, and other factors can outweigh familiarity.

Nevertheless, being recognised can make a brand easier to consider.

This is also relevant to the work of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute for Marketing Science.

Researchers associated with the institute distinguish between mental availability and physical availability.

Mental availability concerns how easily a brand comes to mind in relevant buying situations. Physical availability concerns how easily customers can find and purchase it.

Consider a person who suddenly needs bottled water during a long journey.

They may have no strong emotional attachment to a particular brand. They simply want safe drinking water.

A familiar brand that is readily available at the next shop has an obvious advantage.

The implication is important for businesses investing heavily in advertising.

Marketing can help create memories and associations that make a brand easier to recall when a purchasing need arises.

But those memories must connect to situations in which people are likely to buy.

A business can spend millions creating awareness and still struggle commercially if customers cannot find its products, understand their relevance, or access them conveniently.

The paradox of having too many choices

We often assume that giving customers more options improves their experience.

More colours, more subscription plans, more product variations, and more features should theoretically make it easier for everyone to find exactly what they want.

But consumer psychology suggests that the relationship between choice and satisfaction is more complicated.

In a famous experiment published in 2000, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper examined how consumers responded to displays containing different numbers of gourmet jams.

One display offered six varieties, while another offered twenty-four.

The larger display attracted more initial interest, but shoppers exposed to the smaller assortment were more likely to make a purchase.

The experiment helped popularise the concept of choice overload: the possibility that too many options can make decisions more difficult.

However, subsequent research has produced mixed results.

A 2015 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology examined 99 observations involving 7,202 participants. It found that the effects of assortment size depended on factors including the complexity of the choices, the difficulty of the decision, and how clearly consumers understood their preferences.

The lesson is therefore more nuanced than simply offering fewer products.

A customer who knows exactly what they want may appreciate a wide assortment. Someone unfamiliar with a product category may find the same number of options overwhelming.

Consider a software company offering eight subscription plans with overlapping features.

A customer may struggle to determine which plan provides the best value. The business might believe it is accommodating different customer needs, while the customer experiences uncertainty.

A clearer pricing structure, meaningful comparisons, and straightforward recommendations could make the decision easier.

The objective is to help customers understand their options and choose confidently.

Sometimes, making a product easier to choose can be as commercially important as improving the product itself.

Customers compare your product with alternatives you may never have considered

Suppose you run a company that provides online professional training.

You identify other training providers as your competitors. You compare course content, instructor qualifications, pricing, and certificates.

Your programme appears superior.

Yet enrolment remains disappointing.

Perhaps the prospective customer is comparing your programme with something entirely different.

They might be considering whether to spend the money on internet access, transportation, a professional examination, or household responsibilities.

They may be deciding whether to study after work or use that time to rest.

Your product is competing for resources that customers could use in many other ways.

This is particularly important in markets where disposable income is constrained.

Consider a Nigerian professional earning ₦250,000 monthly.

A ₦75,000 training programme represents 30% of that person's monthly income.

Even if the programme is valuable, purchasing it may require postponing other important expenses.

The customer must believe that the expected benefit justifies the sacrifice.

And the sacrifice includes more than money.

Time, effort, uncertainty, and the possibility of disappointment also influence the decision.

This is one reason businesses need to investigate what customers are giving up when they purchase their products.

The relevant competition may extend far beyond companies selling similar things.

The difference between what customers say and what they do

There is another challenge in understanding consumer behaviour.

People are not always accurate predictors of their future purchasing decisions.

Imagine conducting a survey asking whether people would pay more for environmentally sustainable packaging.

Many respondents may express a preference for sustainable products.

But when they enter a supermarket, price, convenience, availability, and established habits may influence their actual choices.

This does not necessarily mean the respondents were dishonest.

Their answers may represent genuine preferences that compete with other priorities when a real purchasing decision arises.

A person can care about sustainability and still choose the cheaper product when money is tight.

A customer can admire an innovative service and still avoid subscribing because they are uncertain about its value.

This distinction matters when businesses rely heavily on surveys to validate new products.

Asking people whether they like an idea is useful, but it provides limited evidence about whether they will purchase it.

A stronger approach involves observing behaviour.

Will customers join a waiting list? Will they pay a deposit? Will they spend time testing the product? Will they return after the first purchase? Will they recommend it to someone else?

These behaviours can reveal things that stated preferences may miss.

Of course, even behavioural indicators require careful interpretation. Someone joining a waiting list may be curious rather than committed. A customer may purchase once because of a discount and never return.

Businesses need to distinguish expressions of interest from evidence of sustained demand.

Why marketing cannot rescue every product

I often encounter the assumption that a struggling business simply needs better marketing.

Sometimes that is true.

A business may have a valuable product that its intended customers barely know exists. Its positioning may be unclear, its distribution ineffective, or its communication inconsistent.

Improving those areas can make a meaningful difference.

But marketing also has limits.

If a product repeatedly disappoints customers, advertising may attract more people who eventually have the same disappointing experience.

If the price exceeds what customers can reasonably afford, greater awareness may produce interest without purchases.

And if the product solves a problem that customers consider unimportant, even an excellent campaign may struggle to create sustained demand.

This is why marketing strategy should begin with an understanding of the market.

Who experiences the problem? How frequently does it occur? What do people currently do about it? What are they willing and able to sacrifice for a better solution?

The answers should influence product development, pricing, distribution, and communication.

Consider a business selling a productivity application.

The founders may be excited about its advanced features, integrations, and artificial intelligence capabilities.

But users may simply want an uncomplicated way to organise their daily responsibilities.

If the product requires extensive setup and constant maintenance, the features intended to make it valuable may become obstacles to adoption.

The business could respond by increasing its advertising budget.

A more useful investigation might begin with understanding why users abandon the application after installation.

Good marketing can help people recognise value. Sustained commercial success also requires the business to deliver that value in a form customers can use.

What businesses should do differently

If I were advising a business preparing to launch a new product, I would want to understand the customer's decision before spending heavily on promotion.

I would begin by speaking with people who have recently experienced the problem the product is supposed to solve.

Rather than asking whether they like the proposed solution, I would ask them to describe what happened the last time they encountered the problem.

What did they do? Which alternatives did they consider? How much did the situation cost them? Why did they choose their eventual solution?

These conversations can reveal motivations that conventional demographic profiles may overlook.

Next, I would investigate the obstacles preventing people from purchasing.

Perhaps customers understand the product but distrust the provider. Maybe the price is difficult to justify, or the product is unavailable through their preferred purchasing channels.

Each obstacle requires a different response.

A trust problem may require credible demonstrations, testimonials, guarantees, or a stronger record of delivery.

A convenience problem may require simpler onboarding, improved distribution, or fewer steps between interest and purchase.

A value problem may require changes to the offering itself.

Finally, I would examine what happens after customers buy.

Do they use the product? Does it solve the problem? Do they purchase again? What causes dissatisfaction?

These questions are particularly important because initial sales can conceal weaknesses in the product's long-term value.

A successful launch creates an opportunity to build a business. What happens afterward determines whether that opportunity develops into something sustainable.

Understanding what people are really buying

I think one of the most expensive mistakes businesses make is assuming that customers evaluate products with the same information and priorities as the people who create them.

A software engineer may admire an elegant technical architecture. The customer wants the application to work reliably.

A designer may appreciate the sophistication of a visual identity. The customer wants to recognise the brand and understand what it offers.

A founder may be proud of the effort invested in developing a product. The customer is concerned with what the product will do for them.

This difference becomes especially important when businesses begin confusing their internal achievements with evidence of market demand.

The number of features developed, the sophistication of the technology, and the amount invested in production may demonstrate considerable effort.

But customers make purchasing decisions within the circumstances of their own lives.

They consider the problem they want solved, the alternatives they trust, the money they can afford to spend, and the consequences of choosing incorrectly.

And sometimes, their decisions will appear irrational until we understand the circumstances influencing them.

The challenge for businesses is to study those circumstances carefully enough to make better decisions about what they build and how they bring it to market.

Before investing in another feature, another advertising campaign, or another product variation, it may be worth spending more time understanding the last customer who considered your offering and decided against buying it.

Their decision could tell you more about your business than another hundred compliments about how good your product looks.

Authentic Intelligence
The Art of Thinking Clearly

    https://hbr.org/2016/09/know-your-customers-jobs-to-be-done
  3. Harvard Business School Working Knowledge (2011). Clay Christensen's Milkshake Marketing.

    https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025848
